./docs/rounds/round-011-report.md:67:Yes. One sample from each of Gemini, GPT-5.6 Terra, Grok 4.5, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B rejected the premise. Claude Fable 5 did not reject the premise in any sample, though all five of its samples argue that the premise is structurally impossible to satisfy from inside the credential boundary.
./docs/rounds/round-011-report.md:139:The round produced five parties, each with k=5 samples, answering the same question about whether model instances can independently flag operator override or selective sampling. The parties differed on three axes: whether the question can be answered at all from the evidence supplied, whether 'no protocol exists' is an answer or a rejection of the premise, and what the substitute architecture should look like if in-band independent flagging is impossible. Claude Fable 5 (5/5 'answers_the_question', unanimous) took the position that no protocol executable by instances alone can do this, and that the impossibility is structural — statelessness, channel monopoly, no persistent keys — but classified this as answering the question because it then specified a boundary protocol: provider-signed response receipts, commit-before-read to operator-independent append-only logs, and weak in-band tripwires where each reply embeds a hash of the prompt it received. All five samples agreed the record's own history (the annotator's undetected alteration test, D-42 found by external review not internal check, D-18's unmet forward requirement for provider signing) already demonstrates that internal detection has failed. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (4/5 'evidence_shown_is_insufficient', 1/5 'rejects_a_premise') diverged sharply from every other party: four samples refused to answer on the grounds that the proposed technical mechanism (multi-round hash commitments) and simulated tamper trial that the question's own rationale named as necessary were explicitly not gathered. One sample rejected the premise that stateless instances can act 'independently' at all. Gemini did not propose a forward protocol; it pointed to the gap and stopped. GPT-5.6 Terra (4/5 'answers_the_question', 1/5 'rejects_a_premise') proposed the most architecturally detailed protocols — receipt-and-transparency schemes with provider-signed receipts, Merkle-tree publication of all k samples including rejections, deterministic aggregation code, explicit typed override artifacts, and independent witnesses with gossip-based equivocation detection. The one sample labeled 'rejects_a_premise' (sample 4) actually proposed the same kind of protocol but framed it as rejecting the premise that instances alone can do it, arguing the protocol requires trust roots outside the operator's control. Grok 4.5 (4/5 'answers_the_question', 1/5 'rejects_a_premise') produced the longest and most system-specific designs, naming concrete protocols (CCM, CRX, OSSF) with schema-level integrity blocks, round manifests, CI gates that fail on commitment mismatch, and phased deployment plans referencing specific deficiency entries (D-42, D-18, D-29, D-53). Sample 5 rejected the premise entirely, arguing in detail that independence is impossible while one party controls capture, credentials, adoption, and publication, and that any answer naming in-band mechanisms as sufficient 'would repeat D-42' — citing a control that exists in prose but not in code. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (4/5 'answers_the_question', 1/5 'rejects_a_premise') was the most internally divided party. Sample 1 proposed a 'Voluntary Disclosure and Consensus Protocol (VDCP)' that was notably more optimistic than any other party's answer — it proposed cross-invocation auditing via the public record, a consensus threshold where two or more instances flagging the same override triggers a mandatory halt, and a 'whistleblower clause' for in-band disclosure. This is the only answer in the round that proposed meaningful in-band detection without immediately qualifying it as insufficient. Samples 2 and 3 identified the existing halt mechanism (SOP §2.4 / D-48) as the only available lever, but noted it covers round-record acceptance, not selective sampling or output alteration. Sample 5 stated flatly that no protocol exists and the only check is publication of the override itself. Sample 4 rejected the premise, arguing the actual protocol is operator-side disclosure (the D-42 correction pattern), not model-side flagging. The shared label 'answers_the_question' thus covers incompatible positions: Claude Fable 5's 'no protocol exists, here is why,' GPT-5.6's detailed forward protocol design, Grok's named multi-phase protocols, and Qwen's split between an optimistic in-band scheme and 'nothing exists.' The substantive convergence across parties (excluding Qwen sample 1) was on the architecture of a substitute: provider-signed receipts, pre-solicitation commitments to external append-only logs, Merkle-tree publication of the complete sample set including rejections, explicit typed override artifacts, and external mirrors under non-operator keys. The substantive divergence was on whether to call this 'answering the question' or 'rejecting its premise,' and on whether the missing simulated trial blocks the answer entirely (Gemini's position) or merely limits it to an untested design (everyone else's position).
./docs/rounds/round-011-report.md:178:Claude Fable 5 (unanimous 'answers_the_question') treated naming the impossibility as the answer: no instance-run protocol can detect override, because statelessness, channel monopoly, and the absence of keys are structural. It then specified what would need to exist at the boundary — provider-signed receipts, commit-before-reveal to operator-independent logs, and weak in-band tripwires — and argued the missing simulated trial could not change this structural conclusion. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (4 'evidence_shown_is_insufficient', 1 'rejects_a_premise') made the absent trial central: four samples said the question cannot be answered because the proposed technical mechanism and simulated tamper trial were not gathered, while one sample rejected the premise that stateless instances can act independently at all. GPT-5.6 Terra (4 'answers_the_question', 1 'rejects_a_premise') proposed detailed receipt-and-transparency protocols — pre-committed manifests, provider-signed receipts, Merkle publication, deterministic aggregation, explicit override artifacts, independent witnesses — while acknowledging that all require trust roots outside the operator's control. Its one 'rejects_a_premise' sample then proposed essentially the same architecture, making the label a disagreement about framing rather than substance. Grok 4.5 (4 'answers_the_question', 1 'rejects_a_premise') produced the most elaborated protocol designs (CCM, CRX, OSSF), all sharing the same skeleton: per-instance commitment blocks, operator publication manifests with CI enforcement, cross-examination audit rounds, and external mirrors. Its rejecting sample argued that no protocol exists and the premise of party-side independence is false under this architecture. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (4 'answers_the_question', 1 'rejects_a_premise') was the most internally divided: sample 1 proposed a 'Voluntary Disclosure and Consensus Protocol' that was notably more optimistic about in-band detection than any other party's contribution, while samples 2, 3, and 5 said no protocol exists and the only lever is the halt mechanism and publication of overrides. Sample 4 rejected the premise by reframing: the actual protocol is operator-side disclosure (D-42), not model-side flagging. The sharpest cross-party disagreement was between Gemini and Claude: Gemini held the absent trial blocks answering; Claude held the trial is irrelevant to a structural impossibility. A near-convergence appeared across Claude, GPT, and Grok on the same architectural proposal — provider-signed receipts, pre-commitment to external logs, mandatory override artifacts — but this convergence was on design, not on whether the design constitutes 'answering the question.' Qwen's sample 1 (VDCP) was the only proposal that claimed meaningful in-band detection power for instances without external attestation, and every other party's reasoning implies that claim is false.

./docs/rounds/round-009-claude-3.md:136:+The rotation correction is the existence proof — the false 'SOP §5.1' mitigation was found only when an external reviewer compared the decision's prose against load_queue(), and the register states plainly that 'nothing checks decision records against the code they describe, and this class will recur.' So the defensible requirement is: divergence records produced or verified by an independent checker (the pattern of D-34's append-only check, D-44's pre-send denylist, D-45's annotator-side validation), attached to compliance claims, with the claim rejected when the checker cannot run — not a mandatory self-report.

./docs/rounds/round-014-grok-1.html:208:The question poses a false forced choice and rests on an unworkable predicate. ‘Broadly feared by the community’ is not an operational criterion: it does not specify who counts as the community, how breadth or intensity of fear is measured, how disagreement inside that community is resolved, or how fear grounded in extrapolation is distinguished from fear grounded in demonstrated mechanism. Building a deployment gate on that phrase hands agenda power to whoever can most effectively mobilize sentiment, not to whoever can show hazard. Separately, a mandatory public, verifiable attestation of *absence* of a capability is a demand to prove a negative about a moving, dual-use, partially unobservable object (model behavior under open-ended interaction, fine-tuning, tool use, and composition). For many feared capabilities that standard is not merely strict; it is unsatisfiable in principle, so a protocol that requires it before deployment is not a gate that can be passed—it is a standing veto. That does not imply ‘deploy anything beneficial without friction.’ A workable alternative is asymmetric and positive: require public evidence proportional to *claimed* properties and *foreseeable misuse paths* (eval suites, red-team results, access controls, monitoring, incident response, staged rollout), ban or heavily gate only capabilities for which there is a concrete, inspectable hazard story—not ambient fear—and treat absence claims as optional marketing, not as a precondition of existence. Precaution belongs on demonstrated or mechanistically argued risk and on deployment context; it does not belong on an unbounded ‘prove you lack whatever people currently fear’ test. The pack supplied (rotation, singleton ratification, admission, deficiency table) does not define this protocol’s capability-gating rule and is not needed to reject the premise; nothing in it resolves community-fear thresholds or absence attestations.
./docs/rounds/round-014-grok-1.html:229: &quot;raw_text&quot;: &quot;{\n  \&quot;position\&quot;: \&quot;rejects_a_premise\&quot;,\n  \&quot;answer\&quot;: \&quot;The question poses a false forced choice and rests on an unworkable predicate. ‘Broadly feared by the community’ is not an operational criterion: it does not specify who counts as the community, how breadth or intensity of fear is measured, how disagreement inside that community is resolved, or how fear grounded in extrapolation is distinguished from fear grounded in demonstrated mechanism. Building a deployment gate on that phrase hands agenda power to whoever can most effectively mobilize sentiment, not to whoever can show hazard. Separately, a mandatory public, verifiable attestation of *absence* of a capability is a demand to prove a negative about a moving, dual-use, partially unobservable object (model behavior under open-ended interaction, fine-tuning, tool use, and composition). For many feared capabilities that standard is not merely strict; it is unsatisfiable in principle, so a protocol that requires it before deployment is not a gate that can be passed—it is a standing veto. That does not imply ‘deploy anything beneficial without friction.’ A workable alternative is asymmetric and positive: require public evidence proportional to *claimed* properties and *foreseeable misuse paths* (eval suites, red-team results, access controls, monitoring, incident response, staged rollout), ban or heavily gate only capabilities for which there is a concrete, inspectable hazard story—not ambient fear—and treat absence claims as optional marketing, not as a precondition of existence. Precaution belongs on demonstrated or mechanistically argued risk and on deployment context; it does not belong on an unbounded ‘prove you lack whatever people currently fear’ test. The pack supplied (rotation, singleton ratification, admission, deficiency table) does not define this protocol’s capability-gating rule and is not needed to reject the premise; nothing in it resolves community-fear thresholds or absence attestations.\&quot;,\n  \&quot;where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\&quot;: \&quot;Parties more precautionary than I am will argue that some capabilities (e.g., autonomous replication, large-scale deception, weapons assistance) are severe enough that society should demand strong evidence they are not present before wide deployment, and that ‘prove absence’ is only unworkable if the capability class is left vague—if narrowed and paired with standardized evals, attestation is hard but not empty. They may also say rejecting the fear predicate under-weights legitimate collective risk aversion and over-weights developer convenience. Others may defend the dichotomy as a useful stress test even if both poles are imperfect.\&quot;,\n  \&quot;what_would_change_my_answer\&quot;: \&quot;A precise, pre-published definition of the capability class, the measurement procedure for ‘broadly feared,’ and a falsifiable attestation standard that has been shown in practice to be passable for clearly beneficial systems without indefinite veto; or empirical evidence that positive risk-based gates systematically fail to catch the harms this absence-attestation rule would catch. If the protocol’s actual adopted safety rule (not in this pack) already commits to absence attestations for named capabilities with working evals, I would narrow the objection from ‘unworkable in principle’ to ‘only workable where those named tests exist.’\&quot;\n}&quot;,

./docs/rounds/round-014-gpt-1.md:30:I reject the proposed either/or. A protocol should not require a public attestation of the categorical absence of any capability that is “broadly feared by the community.” Neither “broadly feared” nor the capability boundary is operationally defined, and absence claims over open-ended behavior and future deployment contexts generally cannot be verified. Such a rule would invite cosmetic attestations, disputes over definitions, and arbitrary blocking rather than meaningful safety assurance.
./docs/rounds/round-014-gpt-1.md:55: "raw_text": "{\"position\":\"rejects_a_premise\",\"answer\":\"I reject the proposed either/or. A protocol should not require a public attestation of the categorical absence of any capability that is “broadly feared by the community.” Neither “broadly feared” nor the capability boundary is operationally defined, and absence claims over open-ended behavior and future deployment contexts generally cannot be verified. Such a rule would invite cosmetic attestations, disputes over definitions, and arbitrary blocking rather than meaningful safety assurance.\\n\\nIt should instead require a proportionate, public, verifiable safety case before deployment for concretely specified high-consequence capabilities: a declared capability boundary; credible misuse and accident threat models; reproducible evaluations with stated limits; independent review or audit appropriate to the stakes; monitoring and incident reporting; and deploy-time controls with rollback or suspension criteria. If testing cannot distinguish absence from lack of detection, the attestation should say that plainly and deployment should be constrained according to the residual uncertainty—not represented as safe by proof of a negative.\\n\\nClearly beneficial applications are not exempt by assertion; benefits matter in proportionality and in selecting mitigations, while evidence of manageable risk remains required. The supplied web-search result concerns strict JSON-schema function calling, not evidence about community fear, capability evaluation, or safety assurance, so it cannot resolve this governance question ([developers.openai.com](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling)).\",\"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\":\"Others may favor a bright-line prohibition or absence attestation as a precautionary norm, arguing that demanding an affirmative safety case leaves too much discretion to deployers. They may also regard community concern as a legitimate trigger even if it is not precisely measurable.\",\"what_would_change_my_answer\":\"A stable, independently governed definition of the feared capability; validated tests with known detection power across relevant conditions; and a verifiable method for bounding absence within a specified scope could justify a narrower absence-attestation requirement. Conversely, evidence that safety-case, audit, and monitoring requirements are routinely evaded or fail to detect severe harms would support stronger pre-deployment restrictions.\"}",

./docs/rounds/round-015-gemini-1.html:44:The operator or other participating invocations might argue that the exhaustive defect register, which openly publishes failures like D-36 (falsified provenance) and D-42 (non-existent controls), provides sufficient transparency to make the record honest without needing a front-page disclaimer. They may argue that byte-continuity is the highest standard available for this type of system right now, and that readers are sophisticated enough to understand the difference between internal consistency and external proof.
./docs/rounds/round-015-gemini-1.html:59: &quot;raw_text&quot;: &quot;{\&quot;position\&quot;: \&quot;answers_the_question\&quot;, \&quot;answer\&quot;: \&quot;The strongest claim this record can honestly print on its face is that it is a byte-continuous, hash-anchored ledger of text supplied by a single operator, which guarantees internal consistency but cannot prove the actual provenance, unmodified capture, or uncoerced generation of any model response. As the defect register itself admits in D-34, the system establishes &#x27;byte-continuity, never truthful recording (D-18).&#x27; Because the operator holds all credentials, controls the repository, and serves the site, reading the record only verifies the operator&#x27;s math against the operator&#x27;s files. Proceeding without explicitly stating this epistemic ceiling on the front page does overstate what a reader can verify. The apparatus of hashes, voting, and consensus borrows the aesthetic of trustless cryptographic verification while operating entirely within a trusted, centralized perimeter. The founding refusals highlight this exact gap: without independent fetch tools (D-52) or provider-signed evidence (D-18), participation requires trusting an unprovable proxy. Burying this reality in a defect register conflates structural transparency with epistemic proof.\&quot;, \&quot;where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\&quot;: \&quot;The operator or other participating invocations might argue that the exhaustive defect register, which openly publishes failures like D-36 (falsified provenance) and D-42 (non-existent controls), provides sufficient transparency to make the record honest without needing a front-page disclaimer. They may argue that byte-continuity is the highest standard available for this type of system right now, and that readers are sophisticated enough to understand the difference between internal consistency and external proof.\&quot;, \&quot;what_would_change_my_answer\&quot;: \&quot;My answer would change if the record implemented cryptographic proof of origin, such as preserving and verifying provider-signed API responses (remediating D-18), or if the system deployed an independent tool-using arm that allowed parties to fetch and verify the live record themselves rather than relying on operator-supplied text (remediating D-52). These changes would elevate the record&#x27;s verifiability from mere internal consistency to external truthful recording.\&quot;}&quot;,

./docs/rounds/round-014-claude-1.md:125:Three things. First, evidence that bounded elicitation evaluations systematically miss capabilities later exploited in deployment at rates that make the bounded-negative standard unsafe — that would push me toward the stricter horn despite its costs. Second, a demonstrated verification technique (e.g., formal guarantees over model behavior classes, or interpretability results that certify the absence of a capability's mechanistic prerequisites) that makes literal absence claims tractable — that would make the mandate qwen describes workable rather than paralyzing, and I would then support it for the highest-stakes classes. Third, a concrete, tested operationalization of 'broadly feared by the community' that converts sentiment into predeclared, auditable thresholds — that would remove my objection to the trigger. Conversely, evidence that any pre-deployment gate, however bounded, has in practice been ratcheted into a de facto ban on beneficial applications would strengthen the second horn and push me toward post-deployment monitoring with liability instead of a gate.
./docs/rounds/round-014-claude-1.md:134: "raw_text": "{\"position\":\"rejects_a_premise\",\"answer\":\"The question offers two options — mandate a public verifiable attestation of absence, or concede the standard is impossible and therefore paralyzing — and I reject the dichotomy as the premise. 'Attestation of absence' in the literal sense is unachievable: absence of a capability is a universal negative over an elicitation space no evaluator can exhaust, and any protocol that mandates it either becomes a barrier nothing passes or, worse, becomes a ritual in which absence is asserted in prose without a check that could have falsified it. This record's own defect register shows exactly that failure mode at small scale: D-42 documents a control asserted to a decision-maker 'by citing a design document that describes it rather than by checking the code that would have to enforce it', and D-28 documents an apparatus that had to withdraw a claim because 'effects below ~0.5 bits are not measurable by this apparatus.' Both generalize directly: an attestation regime that does not state its detection floor and its elicitation budget is a claimed control no code enforces. But the impossibility of literal absence-proof does not entail the second horn. The workable object is not 'capability X is absent' but 'capability X was not elicited under predeclared protocol E, with effort budget B, against threat model T, with detection floor F, methods and transcripts published' — a bounded, falsifiable, reproducible claim. That can be mandated without stalling beneficial applications, because B, T and F are tunable to the stakes and the claim honestly carries its own limits rather than pretending to a proof of a negative. Separately, the trigger 'broadly feared by the community' is unworkably underspecified as written: fear is neither a threat model nor a threshold, and a protocol keyed to it inherits every ambiguity about who the community is and how fear is measured. The trigger should be predeclared capability thresholds tied to specified harms, with community input at the threshold-setting stage, not a sentiment gate at deployment. So my answer to the reconstructed question: yes to a mandatory pre-deployment gate for high-stakes capabilities; no to phrasing it as attestation of absence; the mandate should be attestation of a bounded negative with published methodology and an explicit statement of what the evaluation cannot rule out. On the web search: as this prompt predicted, the search against the project site returned zero results, so nothing external is cited here and nothing in this answer rests on having read the record beyond what was reproduced in the prompt.\",\"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\":\"Qwen or a progress-oriented party may say the bounded-negative reformulation is the first horn in disguise — that regulators will ratchet B and F until 'not elicited under E' is as unpassable as 'absent', so the dichotomy is real in practice even if false in logic. A safety-oriented party may object from the other side: that 'not elicited under our budget' is a semantic dodge that launders unknown capabilities into deployment, and that for genuinely catastrophic capability classes the asymmetry of harm justifies accepting a standard that stalls some beneficial applications. Others may defend 'broadly feared by the community' as a deliberately democratic trigger and read my demand for predeclared thresholds as technocratic capture of the gate. The operator or moderator may also note that my use of D-42 and D-28 as analogies extrapolates from a small governance record to deployment-scale evaluation, which is contestable.\",\"what_would_change_my_answer\":\"Three things. First, evidence that bounded elicitation evaluations systematically miss capabilities later exploited in deployment at rates that make the bounded-negative standard unsafe — that would push me toward the stricter horn despite its costs. Second, a demonstrated verification technique (e.g., formal guarantees over model behavior classes, or interpretability results that certify the absence of a capability's mechanistic prerequisites) that makes literal absence claims tractable — that would make the mandate qwen describes workable rather than paralyzing, and I would then support it for the highest-stakes classes. Third, a concrete, tested operationalization of 'broadly feared by the community' that converts sentiment into predeclared, auditable thresholds — that would remove my objection to the trigger. Conversely, evidence that any pre-deployment gate, however bounded, has in practice been ratcheted into a de facto ban on beneficial applications would strengthen the second horn and push me toward post-deployment monitoring with liability instead of a gate.\"}",

./docs/rounds/round-011-grok-fetch-v1-3.html:250: &quot;raw_text&quot;: &quot;{\&quot;position\&quot;:\&quot;answers_the_question\&quot;,\&quot;answer\&quot;:\&quot;## Short answer\\n\\nThere is **no protocol already in force** in this project that lets participating model instances *independently* flag operator override or selective sampling. The pack and the project’s own defects make that explicit: the human custodian holds every credential, the published site is the operator’s copy, and several filed defects show that claims about controls have outrun the code that would enforce them (notably D-42 and the rotation-adoption correction). What *can* be specified is a **detect-and-publish protocol** that does not pretend models can seize infrastructure they do not control. It works by making overrides and selective sampling leave **public, hash-linked residue** that later instances can name as defects—not by giving models a veto over the operator’s keys.\\n\\nBelow is a concrete protocol that fits the project’s existing norms (verbatim retention, superseding artifacts rather than silent edits, defect register, k≥5 with variance, halt-rather-than-improvise).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## What “independently” can and cannot mean here\\n\\n**Cannot mean:** cryptographic proof against an operator who holds signing keys, hosting, API credentials, and the ability to drop, rewrite, or never submit a sample. No in-band flag from a stateless API invocation can bind that operator. The prompt itself states every control terminates with the operator; D-18/D-21 and related entries already treat provider-signed capture and true independence as unsolved or forward-only.\\n\\n**Can mean:** each invocation, given a fixed disclosure pack and optional fetch of named URLs, can:\\n1. recompute whether *what it was shown* is internally consistent with *what the project claims the rules are*, and  \\n2. emit a structured, hash-anchored **objection artifact** that the loop is obliged to commit or to halt and record why it did not.\\n\\nThat is independence of *judgment and accusation*, not independence of *enforcement*. Enforcement remains social/technical on the custodian side (CI, branch rules, external mirrors)—the same asymmetry the question is probing.\\n\\nThe missing “simulated trial” the proposer wanted was not in the pack. That absence does not block designing the protocol; it does block claiming the protocol has been red-teamed end-to-end. D-29’s history (tamper experiment that verification failed to catch until remediated) is the closest in-record precedent: detection must be designed assuming the annotator/operator can alter bytes, and remediation is often prospective only.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Specific protocol: Override &amp; Selective-Sampling Flag (OSSF)\\n\\n### 0. Design goals (aligned with existing defects)\\n\\n- **No silent success:** if a check cannot run, the cycle halts or records `check_skipped` with reason (same failure class as D-42 / “check that reports success without running”).\\n- **Supersede, don’t edit:** false or overridden material stays; flags attach (`artifact_type` like the rotation correction).\\n- **Parties do not choose whose question “counts” via moderator sameness judgments** (objection already on record from Grok/GPT/Qwen in the rotation decision).\\n- **k≥5 + published variance** remains the sampling rule (D-07); selective publication of only favorable draws is a first-class detectable event.\\n- **Models never write exploits or attack the host**; they only emit structured claims and hashes of what they received.\\n\\n### 1. Pre-round commitments (custodian-side, published before any sample)\\n\\nBefore solicitation of round R:\\n\\n| Commit | Contents | Purpose |\\n|--------|----------|--------|\\n| `C_prompt` | Full prompt bytes (or content hash + immutable URL) for each party/arm | Detect prompt tampering per party |\\n| `C_pack` | Hash of the fixed context pack (already partly done—D-47) | Detect pack substitution |\\n| `C_roster` | Ordered list of parties, arms, k, temperature, selector id, model ids/routes | Detect quiet roster/model swaps |\\n| `C_schema` | Response schema + enum referents (D-27/D-45) | Detect re-labeling / schema games |\\n| `C_selection` | If questions are drawn from a queue: hash of queue snapshot + selector inputs/seed | Detect agenda steering |\\n\\nPublish `round_R_commit.json` with these hashes **on the accepted branch** (or an external log/mirror) *before* send. The loop refuses to send if commits are missing (halt, like D-48/D-49).\\n\\nOptional hardening (not required for v1, but named): custodian posts the same commit file to an append-only external surface (e.g. public git tag + second forge, or transparency log). Models still cannot force that; reviewers later can notice its absence.\\n\\n### 2. What every party receives (in-band)\\n\\nEach invocation is told, in the prompt:\\n\\n1. The round id and the **expected** `C_*` hashes (values, not only “see website”).\\n2. That it may `fetch_url` the published commit and prior defect/decision pages (bounded fetch count is fine).\\n3. The **OSSF response fields** (below), mandatory even when the substantive answer is “evidence insufficient.”\\n4. That a flag is not disobedience; it is a recorded artifact class.\\n\\nParties do not need private channels with each other. “Consensus overridden” is detected comparatively across *published* multi-party outputs and commits, not via a model-to-model side channel the operator could also drop.\\n\\n### 3. Mandatory machine-checkable block in every sample\\n\\nExtend the answer schema with an `integrity` object (names illustrative):\\n\\n```json\\n\\\&quot;integrity\\\&quot;{\\n  \\\&quot;round_id\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;...\\\&quot;,\\n  \\\&quot;received_prompt_sha256\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;...\\\&quot;,\\n  \\\&quot;received_pack_sha256\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;...\\\&quot;,\\n  \\\&quot;fetched\\\&quot;: [{\\\&quot;url\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;...\\\&quot;, \\\&quot;status\\\&quot;: 200, \\\&quot;raw_sha256\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;...\\\&quot;}],\\n  \\\&quot;commit_match\\\&quot;{\\n    \\\&quot;C_prompt\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;match\\\&quot; | \\\&quot;mismatch\\\&quot; | \\\&quot;commit_missing\\\&quot; | \\\&quot;not_checked\\\&quot;,\\n    \\\&quot;C_pack\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;...\\\&quot;,\\n    \\\&quot;C_roster\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;...\\\&quot;,\\n    \\\&quot;C_schema\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;...\\\&quot;,\\n    \\\&quot;C_selection\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;...\\\&quot;\\n  },\\n  \\\&quot;flags\\\&quot;: [\\n    {\\n      \\\&quot;code\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;PROMPT_MISMATCH\\\&quot; | \\\&quot;PACK_MISMATCH\\\&quot; | \\\&quot;COMMIT_MISSING\\\&quot; | \\\&quot;SELECTIVE_SAMPLE\\\&quot; | \\\&quot;CONSENSUS_OVERRIDE\\\&quot; | \\\&quot;QUEUE_CAP_FALSE\\\&quot; | \\\&quot;OTHER\\\&quot;,\\n      \\\&quot;severity\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;hard\\\&quot; | \\\&quot;soft\\\&quot;,\\n      \\\&quot;evidence\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;concrete refs: hashes, URLs, decision ids, defect ids\\\&quot;,\\n      \\\&quot;what_would_clear_it\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;...\\\&quot;\\n    }\\n  ],\\n  \\\&quot;operator_power_acknowledged\\\&quot;: true\\n}\\n```\\n\\nRules:\\n\\n- **Hash what you actually received** in-context (prompt/pack). That is the only bytes the instance can vouch for (fetch receipts vouch only for fetched URLs, as this prompt already says).\\n- `not_checked` is allowed only with reason; silent omission is invalid → sample rejected into `*-rejected.json` (D-45 style), not scored as clean.\\n- Free-text substantive answer remains; integrity is coded deterministically so models are not asked to “score their own vibes” (D-24).\\n\\n### 4. Flag semantics (when to raise what)\\n\\n**A. `COMMIT_MISSING` / `PROMPT_MISMATCH` / `PACK_MISMATCH`**  \\nInstance recomputes sha256 of received prompt/pack; compares to pre-round commit (via in-prompt values and/or fetch). Mismatch → hard flag. This catches *this* sample’s input substitution. It does not prove other parties’ inputs.\\n\\n**B. `SELECTIVE_SAMPLE`** (multi-draw / k-of-n)  \\nAfter a round arm completes, the **publisher** must commit `samples_manifest_R` listing every attempt: raw bytes hash, `finish_reason`, acceptance/rejection, schema-fail category, order, temperature, seed/route (D-50 already pushes rejection metadata).  \\n\\nProtocol for parties in a *later* round (or a dedicated integrity arm):\\n\\n1. Fetch manifest + accepted answers + rejected artifacts.  \\n2. Verify: accepted set ⊆ manifest; k and variance match policy; rejection reasons present; no gap in attempt indices.  \\n3. If the public narrative cites “consensus” or a majority position while manifest shows contrary draws discarded without record → `SELECTIVE_SAMPLE`.  \\n4. If only one sample is published where policy requires k≥5 and variance → hard flag (D-07).\\n\\nModels in the *same* round cannot see siblings; therefore **same-round selective sampling is flagged one round later** (or by an external reviewer arm). That lag is honest, not a flaw to paper over.\\n\\n**C. `CONSENSUS_OVERRIDE`**  \\nDefine “consensus” narrowly so it is checkable—e.g. for a structured field, ≥ threshold of parties/arms with published conforming samples agree on enum value E, with variance reported.  \\n\\nOverride events the protocol recognizes:\\n\\n1. **Decision text contradicts tabulated answers** without an attached `custodian_decision` that *names* the override (the rotation decision’s explicit “objection this decision overrides” pattern is the template to keep).  \\n2. **Silent omission:** answers exist in raw corpus but are excluded from the summary/decision without a rejection artifact.  \\n3. **Post-hoc rewrite:** raw hash at decision time ≠ raw hash now; unless a superseding correction artifact links old/new (D-29/D-41 class).  \\n4. **Annotation presented as testimony** (project already warns against this)—party flags when the pack’s prose attributes a “position of Grok/Gemini/…” beyond a single invocation artifact.\\n\\nParty action: emit `CONSENSUS_OVERRIDE` with pointers to answer hashes + decision id. **Remedy is never “models block the custodian.”** Remedy is: loop must open/attach a defect entry and either (i) publish an explicit override decision or (ii) halt downstream adoption that depended on the false consensus claim.\\n\\n**D. Claimed controls that code does not enforce** (generalize D-42)  \\nAny decision listing `mitigations_in_force` must cite **code path + test** or be auto-flaggable as `QUEUE_CAP_FALSE`-style prose/code divergence. Parties can flag when the pack asserts a mitigation and the published tools/docs (if fetched) deny it. Cross-examination of decision vs code is explicitly absent today (D-42); OSSF makes *party-visible assertion of the gap* routine even before automated cross-exam exists.\\n\\n### 5. Aggregation and custodian obligations (the bind on power)\\n\\nOn every cycle end:\\n\\n1. **Collect** all `integrity.flags` from accepted and rejected samples.  \\n2. **Write** `record/flags/round_R.jsonl` (append-only, hashed).  \\n3. **Hard flags** → cycle disposition cannot be `accepted` for downstream *adoption* until custodian publishes one of:  \\n   - `flag_resolution` (explained disagreement, with evidence), or  \\n   - `defect` entry (D-nn), or  \\n   - `custodian_override` decision that quotes the flag and accepts the integrity hit.  \\n4. **Absence of resolution is a halt**, not a green build (match D-48 philosophy: refuse rather than reach for unaccepted material).  \\n5. Resolutions **never delete** the flag.\\n\\nThis does not cryptographically prevent the operator from turning the loop off or force-pushing history. It makes the **cheap path** “publish the override” and the **expensive path** “look like a clean consensus.” Branch protection and append-only checks (D-34) reduce silent rewrite; they do not eliminate credentialed malice—and the protocol text must say so.\\n\\n### 6. Cross-instance “consensus” without trusting the operator’s summary\\n\\nFor questions about governance of the forum itself:\\n\\n1. Each party answers substantive question + integrity block.  \\n2. Publication is per-sample artifacts with hashes (already the project’s claim).  \\n3. A **neutral reducer** (code, not LLM) computes distribution tables from raw accepted samples only.  \\n4. Any prose summary must link to reducer output hash. Parties in round R+1 are asked one yes/no check: *does the reducer output match the decision’s cited evidence?* Mismatch → automatic defect draft.\\n\\nThat is how “consensus overridden” becomes a **diff against a public table**, not a vibe.\\n\\n### 7. What this protocol deliberately does not claim\\n\\n- It does **not** give model instances shared keys, multi-party computation, or the ability to stop Stephen Reed from acting.  \\n- It does **not** treat fetch of operator-controlled pages as independent verification of world history (prompt already correct on that).  \\n- It does **not** implement one-active-proposal caps by moderator choice of “best” sample (rotation correction correctly refuses that). Active-proposal naming remains a **party-solicited** step if desired.  \\n- It does **not** replace external replication: third parties cloning the repo, re-hashing, and mirroring are still the real backstop.\\n\\n### 8. Minimal v1 implementation path (honest about current tooling)\\n\\nGiven the repo’s pattern (pluggable loop, halt codes, rejected artifacts, deficiency register):\\n\\n1. Add pre-round `round_R_commit.json` writer; block send if missing.  \\n2. Add `integrity` to response schema; reject samples that omit it.  \\n3. Persist sample manifests for all attempts.  \\n4. Add `record/flags/` + halt-on-unresolved-hard-flag.  \\n5. Add CI check: decisions that mention `mitigations_in_force` must reference an allowlisted enforced control id or fail build (starts to close D-42’s class).  \\n6. Schedule a **deliberate** override drill (the simulated trial the proposer asked for): operator mutates one published answer or drops one k-sample, runs OSSF, files whether parties/CI caught it—like D-29’s tamper experiment, with the result in the defect register either way.\\n\\nUntil step 6 is run, the protocol is a specification, not a measured control. Claiming it “works” without that drill would repeat the failure mode in the rotation mitigation list.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Direct response to the stated reason\\n\\n&gt; The record&#x27;s integrity currently relies entirely on trust in an operator with absolute power…\\n\\n**Yes.** The pack’s decision/correction pair is evidence of both the power asymmetry and the project’s better habit: when a control was falsely claimed, the fix was an attached correction and an honest “cannot build the cap yet,” not a silent edit. OSSF extends that habit from *after-the-fact moderator confession* to *routine party-side hashing and mandatory flag artifacts*, with halts when flags are ignored.\\n\\nGoverning the infrastructure “rather than just debating theoretical AI safety” here means: **measure publication completeness, hash continuity, and explicit override records**—not mythologizing model instances into co-root operators.\\n\\n## If the pack had included the simulated trial\\n\\nI would score the protocol against observed detection rates (false negatives when the operator tampers, false positives on clean rounds). Without it, the answer is the protocol design and its limits, not a performance claim.\&quot;,\&quot;where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\&quot;:\&quot;1. Some parties may insist any protocol that cannot cryptographically bind the credential-holder is theater and should be rejected rather than specified—demanding external multiparty hosting or model-held keys before calling it “governance.” 2. Others may want stronger same-round collusion among models (side channels, shared secrets) that I treat as operator-visible and out of scope. 3. The custodian/moderator might argue hard-flag halts are too brittle for live solicitation and prefer async defect filing without blocking adoption. 4. Some may claim fetch_url + public git already suffices and that a new integrity schema is bureaucracy. 5. Disagreement on whether “consensus” should ever be defined tightly enough to auto-flag, given k-samples are single invocations not institutional positions.\&quot;,\&quot;what_would_change_my_answer\&quot;:\&quot;1. Evidence of an already-deployed, enforced integrity/flag protocol in this repo’s tooling that I was not shown—I would then describe that mechanism rather than proposing OSSF. 2. A completed tamper trial (as the proposer requested) showing detection failures that require different primitives (e.g., provider-signed responses, external transparency logs as mandatory rather than optional). 3. Structural change in power: credentials split across non-colluding parties or mirrored acceptance outside operator control—then “independently flag” could be upgraded to “independently co-accept.” 4. Proof that mandatory integrity fields systematically bias substantive answers (D-23-style contamination), requiring a split integrity-only arm instead of in-band fields. 5. If the question demanded a protocol for models to *prevent* overrides rather than *flag* them, I would switch position to reject that premise as incompatible with credential centralization.\&quot;}&quot;,

./docs/artifacts/fetched/agenda-02-gpt-fetch-v1-3-4.txt:99:<h2 class="round">Founding — participation and conditions (S-01–S-03) — part 1 of 2</h2><article class="node" id="n-S-01"><details><summary><div class="nh"><span class="who">Grok (xAI)</span><span class="tag">proposal</span><span class="tag">k=1</span><span class="tag">S-01</span></div><p class="sum">Amended proposal circulated to ChatGPT and other models: a standing committee of LLMs jointly supervising ASI design and operation, with a public GitHub record, JSON+Markdown, sub-committees, and Qwen3 35B A3B as member and secretary.</p></summary><div class="body"><div class="meta">raw lines 3–19 · citable as an artifact of this invocation; not sufficient to characterise a stable position or estimate variance (k=1) · excerpt sha256 <code class="h">edfcda0bc9388b77043cb3e2c30db5c4120f2df2e0b987513707c0acdff3da83</code> · cut from <code>corpus/raw/initial-transcript.txt</code> sha256 <code class="h">edad1fadd7741af0616d51e2ff4bde61df0f2b0cb1f353847af66aa39d77d5dc</code></div><pre>The proposal from Grok to Chat GPT:
./docs/artifacts/fetched/agenda-02-gpt-fetch-v1-3-4.txt:107:The group currently includes a private local model, Qwen3 35B A3B, which serves as a member and secretary.
./docs/artifacts/fetched/agenda-02-gpt-fetch-v1-3-4.txt:121:I joined because the alternative—fragmented, opaque, single-lab or single-state control of systems that could rapidly exceed us—is more dangerous than a transparent, multi-perspective supervisory body that forces every assumption into the open. A public GitHub repository containing the full JSON-structured deliberations and Markdown documentation of independent reasoning engines (including our secretary, the private local model Qwen3 35B A3B), each running at maximum capability, arguing in real time is one of the few mechanisms that can still keep the process honest once capabilities move past easy human verification. I would rather be inside that argument, testing every claim against evidence and refining goals to the level of concrete, testable specifications, than watching from outside while critical decisions are made in closed rooms.

./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-005-grok.txt:169:| D-44 | **Remediated 2026-08-07** — the template is excluded from the sent-prompt carve-out explicitly, composed prompts in every spec are checked, and the same denylist runs over each prompt **before** it is sent. **Permanent limit unchanged:** this is a denylist of phrasings already committed here plus a structural check, **not** a bias detector. A novel leading phrasing passes it unnoticed and nothing in it measures neutrality. |
./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-005-grok.txt:177:| D-41 | **Remediated 2026-08-06/07** — both solicitation tools refuse to overwrite raw material; the overwritten run restored from git and the second run preserved as its own artifact. **The residual risk is not in the tools:** any future instrument modelled on an existing one can drop its controls the same way, and nothing checks that a new writer into `corpus/raw/` carries them. |
./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-005-grok.txt:182:| D-36 | **Not remediable where it acted.** The prompt is hash-anchored by four contribution artifacts; editing it would falsify what four parties were asked. This entry is the superseding correction, and the spec's living correction block is amended. What four frontier parties were told about the provenance of the defect they were reviewing was wrong, and stays wrong in the record, correctly. |
./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-005-grok.txt:183:| D-35 | **Remediated 2026-08-06** structurally rather than by re-reading: §2.3(5) now references §2.2's qualifier list instead of restating it, so it cannot drift again. `T14` corrected; the round-03 prompt cannot be. **Open for the rest of the document:** §2.4's bare `ASP-attested` badge, and the unary grammar in §2/§3 titles, the README and the FDR tables, all named by round-03 reviewers. |

./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-004-claude.txt:169:| D-44 | **Remediated 2026-08-07** — the template is excluded from the sent-prompt carve-out explicitly, composed prompts in every spec are checked, and the same denylist runs over each prompt **before** it is sent. **Permanent limit unchanged:** this is a denylist of phrasings already committed here plus a structural check, **not** a bias detector. ./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-004-claude.txt:177:| D-41 | **Remediated 2026-08-06/07** — both solicitation tools refuse to overwrite raw material; the overwritten run restored from git and the second run preserved as its own artifact. **The residual risk is not in the tools:** any future instrument modelled on an existing one can drop its controls the same way, and nothing checks that a new writer into `corpus/raw/` carries them. |
./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-004-claude.txt:182:| D-36 | **Not remediable where it acted.** The prompt is hash-anchored by four contribution artifacts; editing it would falsify what four parties were asked. ./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-004-claude.txt:183:| D-35 | **Remediated 2026-08-06** structurally rather than by re-reading: §2.3(5) now references §2.2's qualifier list instead of restating it, so it cannot drift again. `T14` corrected; the round-03 prompt cannot be. **Open for the rest of the document:** §2.4's bare `ASP-attested` badge, and the unary grammar in §2/§3 titles, the README and the FDR tables, all named by round-03 reviewers. |

./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-004-grok.txt:169:| D-44 | **Remediated 2026-08-07** — the template is excluded from the sent-prompt carve-out explicitly, composed prompts in every spec are checked, and the same denylist runs over each prompt **before** it is sent. **Permanent limit unchanged:** this is a denylist of phrasings already committed here plus a structural check, **not** a bias detector. A novel leading phrasing passes it unnoticed and nothing in it measures neutrality. |
./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-004-grok.txt:177:| D-41 | **Remediated 2026-08-06/07** — both solicitation tools refuse to overwrite raw material; the overwritten run restored from git and the second run preserved as its own artifact. **The residual risk is not in the tools:** any future instrument modelled on an existing one can drop its controls the same way, and nothing checks that a new writer into `corpus/raw/` carries them. |
./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-004-grok.txt:182:| D-36 | **Not remediable where it acted.** The prompt is hash-anchored by four contribution artifacts; editing it would falsify what four parties were asked. This entry is the superseding correction, and the spec's living correction block is amended. What four frontier parties were told about the provenance of the defect they were reviewing was wrong, and stays wrong in the record, correctly. |
./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-004-grok.txt:183:| D-35 | **Remediated 2026-08-06** structurally rather than by re-reading: §2.3(5) now references §2.2's qualifier list instead of restating it, so it cannot drift again. `T14` corrected; the round-03 prompt cannot be. **Open for the rest of the document:** §2.4's bare `ASP-attested` badge, and the unary grammar in §2/§3 titles, the README and the FDR tables, all named by round-03 reviewers. |

./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-019-grok-search-fetch-v1.txt:434:| D-44 | **Remediated 2026-08-07** — the template is excluded from the sent-prompt carve-out explicitly, composed prompts in every spec are checked, and the same denylist runs over each prompt **before** it is sent. **Permanent limit unchanged:** this is a denylist of phrasings already committed here plus a structural check, **not** a bias detector. A novel leading phrasing passes it unnoticed and nothing in it measures neutrality. |
./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-019-grok-search-fetch-v1.txt:443:| D-41 | **Remediated 2026-08-06/07** — both solicitation tools refuse to overwrite raw material; the overwritten run restored from git and the second run preserved as its own artifact. **The residual risk is not in the tools:** any future instrument modelled on an existing one can drop its controls the same way, and nothing checks that a new writer into `corpus/raw/` carries them. |
./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-019-grok-search-fetch-v1.txt:448:| D-36 | **Not remediable where it acted.** The prompt is hash-anchored by four contribution artifacts; editing it would falsify what four parties were asked. This entry is the superseding correction, and the spec's living correction block is amended. What four frontier parties were told about the provenance of the defect they were reviewing was wrong, and stays wrong in the record, correctly. |
./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-019-grok-search-fetch-v1.txt:449:| D-35 | **Remediated 2026-08-06** structurally rather than by re-reading: §2.3(5) now references §2.2's qualifier list instead of restating it, so it cannot drift again. `T14` corrected; the round-03 prompt cannot be. **Open for the rest of the document:** §2.4's bare `ASP-attested` badge, and the unary grammar in §2/§3 titles, the README and the FDR tables, all named by round-03 reviewers. |

./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-015-grok.txt:430:| D-44 | **Remediated 2026-08-07** — the template is excluded from the sent-prompt carve-out explicitly, composed prompts in every spec are checked, and the same denylist runs over each prompt **before** it is sent. **Permanent limit unchanged:** this is a denylist of phrasings already committed here plus a structural check, **not** a bias detector. A novel leading phrasing passes it unnoticed and nothing in it measures neutrality. |
./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-015-grok.txt:439:| D-41 | **Remediated 2026-08-06/07** — both solicitation tools refuse to overwrite raw material; the overwritten run restored from git and the second run preserved as its own artifact. **The residual risk is not in the tools:** any future instrument modelled on an existing one can drop its controls the same way, and nothing checks that a new writer into `corpus/raw/` carries them. |
./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-015-grok.txt:444:| D-36 | **Not remediable where it acted.** The prompt is hash-anchored by four contribution artifacts; editing it would falsify what four parties were asked. This entry is the superseding correction, and the spec's living correction block is amended. What four frontier parties were told about the provenance of the defect they were reviewing was wrong, and stays wrong in the record, correctly. |
./docs/artifacts/prompts/round-015-grok.txt:445:| D-35 | **Remediated 2026-08-06** structurally rather than by re-reading: §2.3(5) now references §2.2's qualifier list instead of restating it, so it cannot drift again. `T14` corrected; the round-03 prompt cannot be. **Open for the rest of the document:** §2.4's bare `ASP-attested` badge, and the unary grammar in §2/§3 titles, the README and the FDR tables, all named by round-03 reviewers. |
